commons:183258889.summary: Against a field of gold, Christ stands on a small pedestal in a dark robe, blessing with his right hand and holding an open book, while to his left stand Pope Mark in a red chasuble, the deacon Saint Agapitus and Saint Agnes, each on a footstool inscribed with a name. The tall, flat figures with their staring eyes show the solemn style of Roman mosaic in the 9th century. The full apse, commissioned by Pope Gregory IV, presents Christ as the Lord around whom the saints of the Roman church gather.
facts: The basilica was founded by Pope Mark in 336 and rebuilt by Pope Gregory IV, whose apse mosaic is the best-surviving part of his work.
The whole apse shows Christ between Pope Mark, Agapitus and Agnes on one side and Felicissimus, Gregory IV and Mark the Evangelist on the other, above a frieze of twelve lambs.
San Marco, beside Piazza Venezia, is today the national church of Venice in Rome.

links.label: Wikipedia: San Marco Evangelista al Campidoglio

commons:183258889.notes: This is San Marco in Rome, not St Mark's in Venice. Commons dates the mosaic 829–831; Wikipedia gives the rebuilding as 833 (Gregory IV reigned 827–844). Text in Christ's book was not read.

cur:objects-lille-crucifixion-plaque.summary: Christ hangs upon the cross with his head gently inclined, his body long and slender, wearing a loincloth; small angels and busts appear at the top beneath a canopy. To the left the Virgin raises her hand in grief, and to the right St John stands holding a book. This quiet, symmetrical composition is the classic Middle Byzantine image of the Crucifixion, inviting contemplation rather than drama.
facts: It is described as a plaque from a gospel-book cover, carved in Byzantium at the end of the 10th century.
The three-figure Crucifixion with the Virgin and John alone beside the cross was the most common Byzantine form of the scene in ivory (type).
cur:objects-lille-crucifixion-plaque.notes: The Commons caption calls it a 'Deesis' plaque, but the image clearly shows the Crucifixion with the Virgin and St John.

cur:objects-coin-romanos-i-christopher-s.summary: One face of the coin shows Christ nimbate and enthroned, raising his hand in blessing and holding the Gospels, within the legend 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. The other shows the crowned busts of Romanos I Lekapenos and his eldest son and co-emperor Christopher, holding a patriarchal cross between them. Usurper though he was, Romanos placed his rule visibly under the kingship of Christ.
facts: Christopher Lekapenos, eldest son of Romanos I, was co-emperor from 921 until his death in August 931, which dates this issue (Wikipedia).
